Largescale tongue sole (Cynoglossus arel) reaches a maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], making it one of the larger species within the Cynoglossidae family. Field surveys across the continental shelf waters of the western Pacific have documented individuals approaching this asymptotic size, though such specimens are relatively uncommon in commercial trawl catches. The species exhibits a compressed, ribbon-like body plan characteristic of tonguefishes, with both eyes located on the left side of the head. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis suggest that the ultimate length is attained gradually over several years, with the most rapid elongation occurring during the first two years of life before growth rates decelerate markedly. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Cynoglossus puncticeps indicate that Largescale tongue sole maintains a comparatively larger body size, likely reflecting differences in dietary resource utilization and habitat preferences across the soft-bottom benthic environments it inhabits. This maximum length serves as an important benchmark for fisheries management, as size-selective harvesting pressure can truncate the age structure of exploited populations and reduce the abundance of the largest, most fecund individuals.

Reproductive development in Cynoglossus arel involves a clear size threshold, with the total length at puberty for females recorded at approximately 21.2 centimeters [Lp = approximately 21.2 centimeters], a value that marks the onset of gonadal maturation and represents a critical juncture in the species' life history. Males, by contrast, reach maturity at a notably smaller total length of 19.5 centimeters [Lp = 19.5 centimeters], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism in maturation that is common among flatfishes. Histological examination of gonadal tissue indicates that vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males commence once individuals surpass these critical body sizes, which in turn correspond to specific age classes depending on local environmental productivity. The divergence in maturation length between sexes likely reflects differences in the energetic costs associated with gamete production, with females requiring a larger somatic framework to support the development of high-fecundity ovaries. Population-level data collected from the East China Sea suggest that the puberty lengths are relatively stable across years, though slight variations have been noted in response to fluctuations in food availability and bottom water temperature regimes. These reproductive parameters are essential inputs for estimating spawning stock biomass and for setting minimum size limits in regulatory frameworks.

The wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae of Largescale tongue sole is extremely small, measuring only approximately 0.000092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000092 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume of the fertilised egg, which has a diameter of 0.56 millimeters. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance during the initial endotrophic phase, before the mouth opening develops and first exogenous feeding becomes possible. The extraordinarily low birth mass reflects the typical pattern among marine teleosts that produce numerous small, pelagic eggs as part of a highly fecund, low-investment per offspring reproductive strategy. This initial mass is orders of magnitude smaller than the body weight attained at later life stages, highlighting the phenomenal growth capacity that must be realized during the larval and juvenile phases. The rapid accumulation of somatic tissue is fueled by the consumption of copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton once the trophic switch to active feeding occurs, with growth rates heavily influenced by prey concentration and ambient temperature. The survival bottleneck imposed by this diminutive starting size means that mortality during the first few days post-hatching is exceptionally high.

Female Largescale tongue sole reach an ultimate wet weight of 329 grams [Wwi = 329 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic body mass achieved when somatic growth ceases in the largest individuals, allowing these females to allocate substantial resources to gamete production and thereby contribute disproportionately to population recruitment. This maximum body mass was estimated from length-weight relationships derived from a large sample of mature females collected during research trawl surveys, applying the formula where weight scales approximately with the cube of length. Attaining this mass requires sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates, including polychaetes, crustaceans, and small mollusks, over the course of several growing seasons. The wet weight at puberty for females, marking the body mass at which reproductive maturation is initiated, has been calculated at 47 grams [Wwp = 47 grams] based on the same length-weight relationship applied to the maturation length, a value consistent with that of other similar-sized tropical flatfishes. This nearly seven-fold increase in body mass from puberty to ultimate size indicates that females continue to invest heavily in somatic growth well beyond the onset of reproductive activity, a life-history pattern consistent with an iteroparous, indeterminate-growth strategy. The disparity between pubertal and asymptotic mass also has implications for fecundity, as larger females are capable of producing more numerous and potentially larger eggs, thereby contributing disproportionately to year-class strength.

Incubation experiments conducted at a constant water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] demonstrate that embryonic development in Cynoglossus arel proceeds rapidly, with the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to hatching, being approximately 2.9 days [ab = approximately 2.9 days], and the maximum lifespan observed under these same thermal conditions reaches approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of tropical and subtropical marine flatfishes that spawn in warm waters, where elevated metabolic rates accelerate cell division and organogenesis within the chorionate embryo. This longevity estimate, derived from holding trials where fish were kept under optimal feeding and water quality conditions, likely represents an upper bound for the species, as wild populations may experience shorter lifespans due to predation, disease, and fishing mortality. The combination of a brief embryonic period and a moderately extended adult life places Largescale tongue sole within the demographic category of species that balance rapid early development with a prolonged reproductive window, allowing multiple spawning seasons over the course of an individual's existence.
